sections.model_projection: The model projects Nebraska to win 35.68-13.83, a home margin of 21.86 points, with a projected total of 49.51. Nebraska's win probability sits at 91.2%. The market spread is Nebraska -28.5 with a total of 51.5, meaning the model is about 6.6 points softer on the margin than the market and roughly 2 points under on the total.
sections.offensive_matchup: Nebraska's offense enters with a clear advantage in efficiency: their opponent-adjusted offensive EPA per play (expected points added, a measure of how much each play moves the scoring needle) is +0.19 versus Bowling Green's -0.02, and their offensive success rate — the share of plays that gain enough yards to stay on schedule — is 44.8% compared to BGSU's 33.9%. Nebraska's run game is particularly potent, posting a rushing EPA of +0.14 per carry against a Bowling Green rush defense that has allowed +0.06 EPA per rush. Bowling Green's offense ranks 134th in both offensive EPA per play and offensive rushing EPA, meaning they will struggle to generate consistent positive plays against any competent defense. The Falcons' neutral-script pass rate of 32.4% (131st) signals a heavy run-first identity that Nebraska's defense, despite its own run-defense vulnerabilities, will be prepared to key on.
sections.quarterback_edge: Nebraska's Anthony Colandrea brings 32 career games and 985 career attempts with a 63.6% completion rate and 7.75 yards per attempt, providing a meaningful experience baseline. Bowling Green's Jay Kastantin has just one career game and 30 career attempts, flagged as a player with no prior data for modeling purposes, so the edge calculation falls back to team passing EPA where Nebraska also leads. Colandrea's experience edge is compounded by the fact that Kastantin will be making only his second career start in a hostile Big Ten environment at Memorial Stadium. Nebraska holds a clear quarterback advantage by any available measure.
sections.trenches: Nebraska's offensive line generates 3.29 line yards per rush (20th nationally) in opponent-adjusted metrics, while Bowling Green's defensive front allows 2.82 line yards per rush (70th), creating a meaningful run-blocking edge for the Cornhuskers. On the other side, Bowling Green's offensive line has allowed a sack rate of 6.1% (93rd) against a Nebraska pass rush that generates sacks on 6.0% of dropbacks (73rd), making that a near-wash. The more telling trench story is Nebraska's run defense: their opponent-adjusted defensive rushing EPA allowed is +0.24 per carry (129th), the worst area of their profile, which is the one avenue where Bowling Green's style fit — ranking well in rush-lean versus run defense — could theoretically create some traction. However, BGSU's offensive line generates only 2.72 line yards per rush (101st), limiting how much they can exploit that vulnerability.
sections.explosive_play_edge: Nebraska holds a moderate edge in the explosive play category: their offensive explosive play rate (plays gaining 10+ rushing or 20+ passing yards) is 13.5% (42nd) against a Bowling Green defense that allows explosives at a 13.4% rate (107th). Bowling Green's offense generates explosives on just 11.1% of plays (98th) against a Nebraska defense that allows them at 12.6% (91st). The bigger concern for BGSU is that Nebraska's raw explosive rate from Week 1 was 20.6% (14th), suggesting genuine big-play capability that the opponent-adjusted blend may be understating given Nebraska's weak early schedule (SOS rank 104th).
sections.third_down_red_zone: Bowling Green's third-down defense is a genuine bright spot: they allowed opponents to convert just 28.2% of third downs (7th nationally, opponent-adjusted), which could slow Nebraska's drives if the Cornhuskers face obvious passing situations. However, Nebraska converts third downs at a 49.7% rate (10th), creating a compelling matchup where Nebraska's offense is one of the nation's best at extending drives against a defense that has been stingy on third down. In the red zone, Nebraska scores touchdowns on 70.3% of trips (opponent-adjusted) while Bowling Green's defense allows touchdowns on 68.7% of opponent red-zone visits — both figures flagged as low-sample but pointing toward Nebraska finishing drives. Bowling Green's offense converts only 58.3% of red-zone trips into touchdowns (113th) and averages just 2.98 points per scoring opportunity (123rd), meaning even when they reach scoring position they are likely to settle for field goals or less.
sections.roster_talent: Nebraska holds a commanding talent advantage: their roster talent percentile is 85th with a four-year blue-chip ratio of 30%, compared to Bowling Green's 27th percentile and a blue-chip ratio of 0.0%. This talent gap is the single largest contributor to the model's margin, accounting for over 8 points of projected home advantage. Nebraska's returning production index (0.50) also exceeds Bowling Green's (0.31), meaning the Cornhuskers have more experienced contributors back from prior seasons across offense, defense, and especially receiving (63% returning) and defense (55% returning).
sections.recent_form: Both teams have played exactly one game, so recent form carries no directional signal — the model assigns a neutral edge here with zero form-shift for either side. Nebraska scored 49 points in Week 1 while Bowling Green scored 13, but those raw results are already captured in the efficiency and rating metrics. With only one game of data for each team, all metrics carry inherent small-sample uncertainty, which the model accounts for through its opponent-adjusted blended ratings.

sections.expected_game_script: Nebraska is expected to establish early control through their superior offensive efficiency and talent advantage, with the Cornhuskers' run game (3.29 line yards per rush, 20th) finding consistent gains against a Bowling Green defensive front that has been middle-of-the-pack against the run. Bowling Green's offense, which runs the ball on roughly 68% of neutral-script plays (131st in pass rate) and generates negative EPA per rush (-0.11 per carry, 134th), will struggle to move the chains consistently against Nebraska's defense despite the Cornhuskers' run-defense vulnerabilities. The Falcons' best hope for offensive production lies in the passing game — their raw passing EPA of +0.57 per attempt (35th) was a bright spot in Week 1 — but Kastantin's extreme inexperience and Nebraska's pass defense (opponent-adjusted passing EPA allowed of +0.14, 30th) will limit that avenue. Nebraska's third-down offense converting at nearly 50% should allow the Cornhuskers to sustain long drives and keep Bowling Green's offense off the field, compounding the scoring gap. The game is likely to be decided by halftime, with Nebraska building a comfortable lead that allows them to manage the second half. Bowling Green may find some late-game success against Nebraska's porous run defense if the Cornhuskers play conservatively with a lead, but the talent and efficiency gaps point to a lopsided final score consistent with the model's 35-14 projection.
